newsitem.title: USA: Corn, wheat prices rise, coffee and oil decline.
newsitem.headline: Corn, wheat prices rise, coffee and oil decline.

text.p: Corn prices rose to 4-1/2-month highs Friday as speculators bought actively while coffee prices fell on profit-taking.
In other markets, oil prices closed lower led by gasoline. Copper prices were firm.
Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts closed down 0.13 point at 241.23.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, March corn closed up 4-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.91-3/4, its highest since Oct. 15.

Traders said large professional fund traders remained the major force in the market, buying actively as planting season approaches. Tight world stocks of grains have sparked record rallies in corn and wheat the last two years.
Corn buying by speculative fund investors Friday totaled an estimated 40 million to 50 million bushels, bringing their estimated purchases for the week to over 300 million bushels.
"These guys are relentless," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co., referring to fund buying. "Every day they're buying."
Corn traded as high as $5.54-1/2 last July as worries mounted about dwindling U.S. corn stocks and booming demand.
Wheat also benefited from speculative frenzy Friday, with March wheat closing up 9-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.73.

Traders said world wheat supplies looked in much better shape this year than last, although worries about spring wheat planting delays due to heavy snows in the northern Midwest and low winter wheat plantings last fall were supportive.
But professional speculators, with buying tied to the expiration of March wheat options, were a big factor Friday.
"This is not fundamental," said Skip Searcy of FIMAT Futures. "There was a lot of buying against expiring options."
The CBOT March options expired at midday Friday, leaving open the potential for a late race to the $3.70 strike or exercise price in the March futures. That fed the rally, traders said.
Weekly export sales of wheat reported by the Agriculture Department totaled 287,200 metric tons, near the high end of expectations for 250,000 to 300,000 tons.

Soybeans and soymeal prices closed lower on widespread talk that China, a major soymeal importer for its meat industry, had canceled or switched 450,000 metric tons of recently purchased soymeal from South America and India.
March soybeans closed down 3 cents a bushel at $7.83 and March soymeal down $1.80 a ton at $257.60.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March coffee closed 3.65 cents a pound lower at 174.80 cents as traders took profits by selling contracts bought earlier in the rally.
"It's Friday and it has been a volatile week," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "I think people were reluctant to hold their positions over the weekend."

Coffee prices are still up 70 percent since the first week in December, fed by tight physical stocks at coffee roasters in the Northern Hemisphere, reduced shipments from coffee-producing nations under an export quota agreement, and worries about the bellwether Brazilian crop -- as much as 40 percent of world supply -- due to be harvested starting in July.
Copper prices rose, with March copper ending 1.85 cents per pound higher at 113.85 cents on the COMEX division of the New York Mercantile Exchange.

March copper rose above $1 a pound just before the end of the year and has worked higher since, with analysts pointing to smaller world stocks this year as supportive. So traders Friday shrugged off a modest rise of 1,875 metric tons in London Metal Exchange weekly stocks at 222,500 tons.

Traders had expected a dip of at least 3,000 metric tons. "Although stocks on LME rose this morning, it was a generally bullish number," said analyst Fred Demler of E D and F Man International, who added that a downward revision by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics in global producer stocks totals should prompt an upward revision in price forecasts.
Oil prices at the NYMEX were led lower by gasoline on the prospect of more supply, as a large refinery owned by Tosco Corp. was expected to be restarted sooner than expected.
The union for workers of Tosco's Marcus Hook refinery in Pennsylvania said the 150,000-barrel-a-day facility was set to restart in April, three months early, after major renovation.
The company later denied the April start but said it was spending about $50 million to upgrade the refinery.

Unleaded gasoline for March delivery settled at 61.82 cents, down 0.96 cent per gallon, while March heating oil fell 19 cents to 57.85 cents a gallon. April crude oil futures closed at $21.39 a barrel, down 30 cents.
